MESSAGE FROM YUKON GOVERNMENT-BEAUFORT SEA DRILLING RIGHTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Secretary of State for External Affairs who has just made a rhetorical flourish of defending Canadian sovereignty. Will he confirm that he has received a telex from the territorial Government of the Yukon which says: "You appear to be ignoring a serious threat to jurisdiction over our Arctic". The telex goes on to state: "I fail to understand your reluctance to come to grips with this important issue".
Those are very serious charges from a respected and responsible Government in our country. What does the Government intend to do about them? How does it intend to respond to the very serious allegations by the Government of Yukon that it is failing to defend Canadian sovereignty with regard to drilling rights in the Beaufort?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: MESSAGE FROM YUKON GOVERNMENT-BEAUFORT SEA DRILLING RIGHTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I cannot confirm whether there has been received in my office a communication from the Government of the Yukon. Naturally, if there has, I will consider it and treat it with respect as I do communications from that and other Governments.
The question at issue is the hearings which are being held with regard to the environmental impact of possible oil and gas activity in the Beaufort Sea. I have today sent a letter of protest to the Government of the United States with regard to that action because it has to do with hearings dealing with an area east of the 141st meridian.
I should advise the Member, as I think I did yesterday, that a similar protest was issued on an earlier occasion when an action of hearings was commenced in the United States. The consequence of Canada's protest at that time was that bids with respect to the disputed area were neither accepted nor rejected. Leases were not issued. I hope that our protest this time will have the same effect.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask the Secretary of State for External Affairs about that very issue, the representations we are making to the U.S. administration. There have already been two hearings held and two more are scheduled. In his note of protest did the Minister specifically ask that the hearings now being conducted be stopped until this particular issue is resolved and the Canadian rights to those territories are clearly identified? Have we asked the U.S. to stop holding hearings over our territory?

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I cannot say with confidence that we know all of the routes which might be taken, particularly by Soviet submarines, if they are in the Arctic. should have at least followed the traditions followed in all committees where you go to all Parties in turn.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to draw to your attention an attitude of this Government which I feel is absolutely improper. This is not the first time that committee chairmen, who are all Government Members, follow a procedure that flies in the face of a rule that has prevailed in this House for years, namely that the Chairman should alternate from one Government Member to one Opposition Member. Now we see that in a number of committees of this House, the chairman does not follow that rule and assigns the floor to Government Members in succession without recognizing Opposition Members. As you know, Mr. Speaker, this Parliament is rather exceptional in the sense that the number of Opposition Members is very limited, and I would appeal to your sense of fairness in defending the interests of Opposition Members. There are very few of us in this Parliament but still we have a right to be heard. So in the committee process we should be recognized as often as Government Members.
What has happened, what went on this morning is not one single occurence. It is a situation that has been arisen on a number of occasions, wherein a Conservative chairman has failed to recognize an Opposition Member right after a Government Member. This means an Opposition Member often has to wait for an hour, and hour and a half before he is allowed to carry on with the questionning and do his duty, which is to ask questions from the Government as an Opposition Member.
I feel that this situation has been going on for too long, and I would appreciate it if the Chair could look at this practice that is prevailing in committees of the House, and have instructions issued to committee chairman who, as it happens, are all Government Members and, who perhaps without realizing it, are taking advantage of the Conservative Party's overwelming majority in this Parliament.

Mr. Speaker, if I may add to what has already been said by my colleague for Papineau (Mr. Ouellet), we are talking about something which has always been a tradition. I recognize that we now have a new Parliament and a great many new committee chairmen, but I believe that the tradition should still be followed and that it would be appropriate to remind Hon. Members and all committee chairmen how we have been doing things for a great number of years. For my part, I had the honour to chair the Committee on External Affairs and National Defence for nine years.
Whatever the circumstances, and I can see the former Minister of National Defence in the House, the first questioner was always a member of the Official Opposition and we always had a first round of questions from both the opposition parties and the Government. After that, I recognize that, with the incredible majority held by the Government, a greater
Privilege-Mr. Rodriguez
proportion of Government Members should be able to speak. This is a principle of fairness which I would be the first to defend. If Your Honour feels the need to comment the matter today, you could perhaps ask the Committee on Management and Members' Services, which is made up of all the committee chairmen, to examine this issue. I believe that this could be done. We shall be meeting this afternoon at 5 o'clock, I think. This is the committee which is composed of committee chairmen. I undertake to raise this question because it is a matter of equity, and I am sure that the Government will realize that our traditions must be followed.
On the other hand, I am fully aware that, with its enormous majority, the Government should not have to feel disadvantaged because of the need to have complete rounds all the time in view of the small number of opposition members. However, for the first round of questions, our traditions should be maintained and one representative from each opposition party should be able to ask questions. I would even say that the first to ask a question could perhaps be the representative of the Official Opposition, and if there is no agreement, one representative of the Government majority, and immediately after, a representative of the New Democratic Party. Then, we could proceed in such a way as to restore the balance among the various parties. I think that Your Honour should remind the House about the basic principles of equity. As long as there are no abuses from the two Opposition Parties, I also believe that, on principle, the very first to be recognized should be the representative of the Official Opposition. Personally, I would have no objection if the second questioner were a Government member, but the third definitely should be. I would prefer it to be, in order, the Official Opposition, the New Democratic Party and the Government. However, if this does not meet the wishes of the majority, we could perhaps proceed equitably in the following manner: First, the Official Opposition, since this is the established tradition for Parliamentary Committees, second, either an opposition member from the New Democratic Party or a Government member on condition that the Chairman immediately afterwards recognize a member of the New Democratic Party. I believe that this is the only way to be fair to the Government majority while preserving our traditions.

Mr. Speaker, I think it is important for you to appreciate that each commttee must set its own rules in this area and that there is no appeal to the House as a whole unless there is disorder.
The Standing Committee on Public Accounts, which is chaired by a member of the Official Opposition, operates on exactly the same principle as my colleague who is Chairman of the Standing Committee on Labour, Employment and Immigration. However, it is important for Your Honour to realize that each committee deals with a different topic in a vast government array and has to work out these matters for

itself. The process within a committee might be different, depending upon whether the committee is studying the Estimates or annual reports, which may tend to be more Government versus opposition with us wanting to stick to the traditional mix, or whether it is studying new policies under the new Standing Orders.
The idea behind the new Standing Orders was to get Members of Parliament, all of whom are equal, addressing themselves to a problem. When Members start to look at a problem as a problem Party differences are evident. The objective was that the committee would then come up with unanimous recommendations. It may be that in new policy areas the committee itself would decide to be much less partisan and the rotation of speakers would be quite different.
My point is that each of these matters has to be worked out by each member of the committee, and it will depend upon the chemistry of the committee. If opposition Members play tricks or the Government plays tricks on opposition Members, the committee will be poisoned and it may not work as well. However, it is not for Your Honour to become involved at this point. It should be left to each committee to work out, and it should only come before Your Honour if there is grave disorder.

Mr. Speaker, I do not want to repeat some of the very important comments which have been made on this point. However, I should like to add another element. I urge Your Honour to recall that we are at a rather important point. When the provisional Standing Orders were before us, we experienced a number of new ways to make Parliament and its operations more effective and more efficient. We tried different approaches as part of the changes to the Standing Orders to improve the work of the committees. By and large there is recognition that the committees are working more effectively and more efficiently than perhaps they ever have.
I can recall many occasions when a government Member, a chairperson, and a member of the opposition Parties were the only participants in a committee. I remember them staying for long periods of time to keep the quorum so that important witnesses could be heard. That occurred time after time. Committees work like the House of Commons, if there is a sense of co-operation and willingness to work and if a sense of fairness overrides the business being conducted.
When the committee of chairpersons meets later today, I urge it to consider the important leadership roles exercised by chairpersons. It is the chairperson who creates a certain tone in the committee and sets the atmosphere in which the committee operates. Because the Government always has a majority of members, it can exercise its power and might at its discretion. However, it does so at its peril.
I urge Hon. Members to recognize that if we are to make Parliament work and to make it a productive, positive place in which to conduct the business of the Government, it is important, particularly for those who are in a position to do so,
to ensure a sense of fairness. Not only must there be fairness, but there must be a perception that fairness exists in committee. When one considers the actions taken by government Members and the chairperson who were present this morning, one could question whether or not there was a perceived sense of fairness for the work the committee was attempting to complete earlier today.
In the best spirit of co-operation, fairness and productivity, Mr. Speaker, I urge you to consider communicating in an appropriate way to the committee chairpersons not to dictate how they proceed or conduct the affairs, but simply to remind them of the very responsible role they have in making Parliament and its committees function well.

speakeroldname: Mr. Pierre Blais (Parliamentary Secretary to Deputy Prime Minister and President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Deputy Prime Minister; Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, however challenging the matter raised by the Hon. Member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Rodriguez), I should like to seek the guidance of the Chair on a specific point, Mr. Speaker.
The Hon. Member for Nickel Belt has raised this point under a question of privilege, and then in the following minutes several Members referred to points of order. We then learned from other Members that this matter was raised in a standing committee and led to a vote. As I understand it-and this is where I seek guidance-our Standing Orders do not allow a Member to rise in the House and comment on committee proceedings which led to a vote.
I would suggest that we are now debating a wide-ranging topic, but that the matter has been settled and that, technically, we are not allowed to refer to it.
Since I have few opportunities to do so, I listened to you very closely a moment ago and I always do my best to become familiar with our proceedings here in the House. Anxious to learn as I am, I simply wanted to focus on what appears to me to be a slippery point, namely that Hon. Members rise just about any time on questions of privilege and points or orders on a wide variety of issues, then we spend one or two hours debating practically every incident likely to happen inside and outside the House as well as in committees.
I am trying to learn our Standing Orders. We operate under provisional Standing Orders and I think the Chair should indeed apply them with some flexibility, but not to such an extent that Hon. Members might even rise in the House on points which are out of order. The Hon. Member for Nickel Belt has more experience than I and he ought to know better.
Hon. Members should not always seek the floor on doubtful questions of privilege precisely because in view of their significance our privileges are to be strictly observed and we much rise only when it is indeed a matter of privilege.
December 9, 1986

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at first glance this may seem to be something that involves a rather small point to be decided within a committee itself, but I submit that what we are talking about here really involves something that is important to the operation of the House of Commons as a whole. If this House of Commons is to operate increasingly through committees and not to be limited in its work primarily to that which is done within this Chamber, then what happens in committees has to be fair and has to be seen to be fair with respect to all Members of the House.
Committees do not belong to the Party which, for the time being, forms the majority in this House, anymore than the House of Commons itself belongs to members of the Party which, for the time being, has the majority of Members of the House. The results of an election, even an election that gives a Party a substantial majority, does not mean the creation of a one-party state. There is a role in the House of Commons and, therefore, in its committees for all Members of the House, and our parliamentary system gives a special role to those Members forming the Opposition Parties, particularly the members of the second-largest party, that forming the Official Opposition. Any attempt to destroy, weaken or distort that traditional concept is something that could weaken, distort and ultimately destroy the concept of parliamentary government itself.
I can recall over the years in the many committees in which I participated that it was always traditional, and accepted when the Conservatives were on the Opposition side of the House, that their spokesperson always led off, and very soon thereafter, as soon as such a spokesperson was available, a representative of the New Democratic Party was heard. It was never suggested when there was a Liberal majority on the committee that representatives of the Conservative Party or the New Democratic Party would not be heard until all Liberals who wanted to speak would be heard. This was never done. It was not even suggested. I have not heard one word why that practice suddenly becomes wrong now that the Conservatives form the Government. If that practice was right when the Conservatives were in Opposition, then it continues to be right today.
I conclude with this point, Mr. Speaker: We are operating now under new rules, but these rules are in place only on a trial basis. They do not extend beyond the end of this year without the consent of this House. I give warning to people on the Government side that if they want those rules to continue they had better give evidence right now that they do not intend to operate this place like the organ of a one-Party state. They better give evidence that they are ready to have this place operate fairly in a way which recognizes the traditional role of Opposition Members or, and I say right now, they will have a very difficult time getting those rules extended. I have put this warning on the record, and I hope the Conservatives pay attention to it.
Privilege-Mr. Rodriguez

Mr. Speaker, as you know I have only been a Member of this House for some two years. However, during that time I have served as a full-time and regular Member and as a part-time Member on a number of committees of this House standing, legisative and otherwise. If there has been one thing that has struck me as significant in comparison with committees on which I have served in other places in the past dealing with Government affairs and the governing of this country, it is the fact that there seems to be a great tradition in standing committees and other committees of this Parliament not to start on time. For some reason or other people take it as their given right and tradition not to start and not to be there on time or to start on time. As a result, I and other Members of Parliament have had to wait, often for half an hour or three-quarters of an hour, sometimes an hour, before starting a committee meeting because people have not been there to get the meeting under way.
It seems to me that the criticisms we are hearing this afternoon about the breach of a tradition of this House about who speaks or who has the opportunity to ask questions first and last always can be corrected in one very simple way. If all of the members of that particular committee took their responsibilities very seriously and decided to get to the meeting on time, there would be no question about that long-standing tradition being followed.
I would like to concur with the statement of the Hon. Member for Windsor West (Mr. Gray), the House Leader for the Opposition, who says that what has to happen in committee meetings is that things have to be done in a fair way and in a way that seems to be fair. I would suggest that if all Members of Parliament, including Members of both Opposition Parties, got to committee meetings on time there would be no question, either in the Standing Committee on Labour, Employment and Immigration or any other, about the fairness of the allotment of questions. I urge all Members to get to committee meetings on time.
I know that the Hon. Member for Calgary West (Mr. Hawkes) who chaired the committee about which we are talking this afternoon would be happy to let the Hon. Member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Rodriguez) ask questions after the Hon. Member for the Liberal Party, as long as they were both there to start their questioning at the appointed time.
I was there.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: The Chair is concerned that discussion of this point, which is important, as Hon. Members have heard, not go on for too long. I will recognize one more Member. The Member for Cochrane-Superior (Mr. Penner) has been trying to get the floor.

Mr. Speaker, I will not repeat any of the arguments which have already been made. I wholeheartedly support the contention of my hon. friend from Nickel Belt that the Parties must be recognized in

December 9, 1986
Privilege-Mr. Rodriguez
committees. Comments made by the Hon. Member for Lethbridge-Foothills (Mr. Thacker) caused me to rise. Although he did not say it specifically, he came rather close to expressing a wish that we had a congressional committee system within a parliamentary system. I understand that yearning because I have been so tempted myself on occasion. However, I say very simply that it will not work. As long as we have a parliamentary system, our committees must respect that parliamentary system and recognize that it cannot be congressional in nature. That leads me to my point.
Because our committees are parliamentary in nature, we cannot impose upon them a system which allows for the precedence of seniority in the recognition of members or for members to be recognized in order of regions. We must always begin with the recognition of the three political Parties, the Official Opposition, the Government, and then the New Democratic Party, in that order, or a slight variation thereof as the Hon. Member for Saint-Denis (Mr. Prud'homme) suggested.
As much as some Members may wish to have a different system for committees, it will not work. We are all part and parcel of the same system. We must learn to live with it. This is the parliamentary system and in the parliamentary system the political Parties must be recognized as they are in the House under your leadership, Sir. That is much more than a tradition. It is the heart of the parliamentary system itself.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I indicated that I would hear only one more Member. However, I did not realize that the Hon. Member for Victoria (Mr. McKinnon) had been seeking the floor. I think all Hon. Members would agree that he should be heard.

Mr. Speaker, I am inclined to agree with you that we have had quite a conversation on this subject. I do not think for a minute that it is a question of privilege, but it is an issue which is deeply felt by several people.
I rise mainly to confirm what the Hon. Member for Saint-Denis (Mr. Prud'homme) said. He chaired the Standing Committee on External Affairs and National Defence for nine years and unfailingly recognized me first. I had not thought it was because I was a Conservative. I thought it was because of the high quality of my questions which started the committee hearings on a high intellectual level.
However, we must be fair. I agree with the protests that have been made that we should alternate from side to side. However, with such a majority in one Party it would mean that the fifth Conservative has to wait while three Liberals speak and three New Democrats speak before he gets his first chance. I think many chairmen have worked out a very satisfactory system. The Official Opposition is recognized first, the Government second and the New Democratic Party third. Three or four government Members are then recognized. That is a reasonable compromise. I think this has been a worthwhile discussions.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I want to thank all Hon. Members for their interventions. While the Hon. Member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Rodriguez) was making his remarks I indicated that I did not think this was a question of privilege. However, I do take this as a grievance and a serious matter. I have listened carefully to what has been said.
I want to thank the Hon. Member for Victoria for his comments because those Members who have had a lot of experience in this Chamber have something very important to contribute on these matters. That applies to some other Hon. Members who have spoken, especially the Hon. Member for Saint-Denis (Mr. Prud'homme). I believe it is appropriate that I make it clear that there is no question of privilege. However, I return to the commitment I made some minutes ago. I will draft an appropriate letter setting out the basic things that have been said in this debate. I will send that letter to committees and ask them if they would please address the matter.
The Chair has had occasion, and probably will again for some time into the future, to remark that the spirit of reform which has made changes in the committees is of great interest and importance to all Hon. Members. There is naturally a tendency, when matters cannot be settled in committee, to bring them to the floor. The Hon. Member for Bellechasse (Mr. Blais) said that he wished some guidance from the Chair on these matters. I can guide the Hon. Members and others by saying that in a strictly legalistic sense perhaps the rule has been abridged a little this afternoon through a lengthy discussion. However, as Hon. Members know, we do not rule this place completely and strictly in a legalistic sense. The Chair is guided by the sentiments and expressions of intention of Members in the Chamber.
I hope Hon. Members will feel that I have paid attention to the sense in the Chamber that this is an important matter and that Hon. Members wished to be heard. The Chair will do its best to bring the concerns expressed to the attention of the appropriate committee chairmen and others. I hope those actions will help all Members to do the work which must be done.
I hope that there will be no need for anyone in this Chamber to give warnings about the possible extension of many of the rules. With direct reference to what the Hon. Member for Windsor West (Mr. Gray) said, it is very important that Hon. Members come to agreement on these rules. I think all Hon. Members would agree with the Chair that it would be a step backward if we were to enter the last period of provisional rules feeling that the success which might have been made of the reforms has not met all expectations.
The Chair is cognizant of what has been said. Again in reference to what was said by the Hon. Member for Bellechasse, there is a time when the Chair allows some latitude and I believe that this afternoon was an appropriate occasion for it. I thank all Hon. Members.

Hear, hear!
December 9, 1986
